t: ‘I thought I could outsmart biology’: more and more women are freezing their eggs – but what happens next?
lede: The procedure has never been more popular, with high-profile women such as Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez publicly getting in on the act. But outcomes vary. Women around the world tell their stories

img.cap: Jessica Long has had successful IVF with eggs frozen after a relationship ended. Photograph: Flora Hanitijo/The Guardian

From a medical perspective, oocyte cryopreservation (more commonly known as egg freezing) is a lengthy and often expensive procedure. It begins with a slate of scans and blood tests, followed by a course of self-injected hormones to stimulate the ovaries. After 10 to 14 days, patients undergo surgery to extract their available eggs. Treatment cycles vary widely in price, with the whole process costing about £3,850-£4,850 in the UK, $10,000-$20,000 in the US and $7,000-­$12,000 in Australia, depending on location and individuals’ health insurance policies, and not including ongoing storage or later implantation costs. Many people need several rounds to reach their desired number of eggs, as the greater the number, the greater the chance of eventual success with fertilisation and transfer.

The procedure can be physically and financially gruelling, but more people are freezing their eggs than ever before. p: Dr Lindsay Kroener, an associate clinical professor in reproductive endocrinology at the UCLA David Geffen School of Medicine, attributes the rise to several factors: delayed childbearing due to career, finances or not yet having a partner; greater visibility of the procedure through social media and clinic marketing; and some employers offering fertility support. The availability of egg freezing has changed the course of many lives – but not always in the ways people had hoped.

Software engineer and startup founder Jessica Long froze her eggs after a long-term relationship ended. She was 31 and reluctant to pause an exciting career and social life that spanned Silicon Valley and Senegal. “I thought freezing my eggs would give me an insurance policy,” she says. “I could defer the urgency I was feeling and date men my age without projecting a sense of desperation around fertility timelines.”

Before she froze her eggs, “there was a chronic anxiety loop in my mind”, she says. “What if I can’t get pregnant? What if I’m losing my last years of fertility? What if my partner waits too long before committing to parenthood and this possibility slips away for ever? Once I froze my eggs, I felt a deep sense of peace.”

Speaking to people who have frozen their eggs, the idea of “insurance” comes up again and again. “Wanting to reduce anxiety and keep your options open is a completely reasonable motivation for egg freezing,” Kroener says, but “it is important not to let this create a false sense of security. Egg freezing is expensive and may take multiple cycles to have a reasonable payoff. I would think of the cryopreserved eggs as a backup plan, but not a guarantee.”

Sarah, 44, works in education in Australia. A decade ago, when she was in her early 30s, she froze her eggs while working in the IVF industry. Her background meant she entered the process with a strong understanding of what it would involve. “I had conversations with my colleagues and my doctor, and knew you probably needed 10 to 20 eggs to have a good chance of having one live birth,” she says. Across two cycles, she managed to freeze 24 eggs. “I thought it was a good result. It made me feel really confident I would be able to have at least one child from that cohort.”
A few years later, she met her husband and they easily got pregnant with their first child. But when trying for a second, they faced complications, including three miscarriages over 18 months.

During this stressful time, Sarah took comfort in knowing she’d successfully frozen her eggs when she was younger. At first, the process of using them went well. “They all thawed beautifully, they were all alive, they were inseminated and 10 were fertilised.” But none of the fertilised eggs became embryos. “They all stopped growing at around the two- to four-cell stage, so very early on. I was really shocked about that.”

Another attempt was also unsuccessful. “It was absolutely devastating, I was gutted. It felt like another pregnancy loss. Even though, as a scientist, I know there are no guarantees, I still thought the probability of me having at least one baby from those eggs was very high. To not even get to an embryo transfer phase was just mind-blowing. I couldn’t reconcile that it didn’t work.

“There were a lot of emotions to unpack,” she says. “I’d made life decisions based on having those eggs in the freezer.” She feared her decision to wait may have robbed her of the chance to have another child, but two years ago the couple had a daughter conceived naturally. “It’s funny because, with hindsight, what the frozen eggs did was give me this sense of hope and freedom that I would not have had otherwise,” Sarah says. She believes that “freedom” helped her meet her husband. “Even though the process didn’t work, and it was really disappointing and felt like a waste of time, I wouldn’t be where I am now without it.”

Kroener is keenly aware of the physical, emotional and financial toll of any fertility procedure when discussing options with her patients. “I talk through when she plans to have children, how many she wants, whether she has a partner or would consider the use of donor sperm, and what her testing shows about her egg quantity. We also discuss cost, side-effects and realistic success rates, based on age and egg quantity.”

She is conscious that increased messaging and marketing around egg freezing can create pressure and expectation. “My job as a physician is to paint a realistic picture for each patient: what egg freezing can and cannot do, the costs and the chances of success. Seeing a fertility doctor about egg freezing shouldn’t feel like a sales pitch. It should be a chance to explore your options and feel supported in making the right decision for you, including deciding not to do it.”

Devaki Wallooppillai, 34, a physician from Perth, froze her eggs before having surgery for endometriosis in 2023. “Egg freezing is often presented in less than nuanced ways,” she says. “Either it’s sold as empowerment, a neat solution to the biological clock, or it’s framed through scary fertility statistics. Neither alone helps someone make a good decision.”

Before freezing her eggs, Wallooppillai had been in a 10-year relationship that ended in divorce. Although it was a difficult time, she says the breakup “helped me be more open-minded about possibilities in the future, including raising a family”. She hadn’t always been certain she wanted children, but with her health complications, she foresaw “potential difficulty down the line”. While she didn’t know what her future would look like, “I did know that if I let the window close without trying, I would regret it intensely”.

A few years later, Wallooppillai met her husband and was conscious of how her earlier choice reduced the pressure to move quickly. When they decided to start a family, the couple underwent IVF with fresh embryos, as these were “more likely to implant than thawed eggs”. Their daughter was born earlier this year, and although the frozen eggs weren’t used, they still serve a purpose, she says, “as a later resort”.

Egg freezing is often recommended for women experiencing other health issues, which means it can be physiologically, as well as emotionally, complex. Ten years ago, Canadian government worker Niamh Harraher froze her eggs at 40 after being diagnosed with breast cancer. “It was clear I was going to need chemotherapy, which can put you into early menopause and leave you infertile.” The surgeon who performed Harraher’s mastectomy “was very positive about the prospect of fertility treatment and encouraged me to investigate it”.

Egg freezing might solve one problem for Harraher, but it created others. She had hormone-driven breast cancer, so her oncologist was concerned that pregnancy might mean stopping key anti-recurrence medication. Harraher went ahead anyway. “When I froze them, I wasn’t 100% sure what I’d use them for. I was deep into cancer treatment and just living day to day, really focused on trying to get better.” After diagnosis and aggressive treatment “in very quick succession”, she says, “losing a breast and losing my ability to become a mother all at once was just too much loss for me to face at that moment”.

Ultimately, she decided against attempting pregnancy, but the eggs still gave her a sense of control. “People might hear my story and think, oh, what a shame, she went through cancer and all of that trouble to harvest her eggs and freeze them, and then she didn’t use them. But I was able to make decisions about whether or not to have a child on my terms.

Cancer didn’t rob me of the ability to be a mother,” Harraher says. “I had a pathway but I chose not to use it, and that is very different from having your ability to reproduce taken from you in a situation where you’re already terrified and grieving and sick.”

Now 51, she says the experience involved significant grief, but also brought comfort. “I do have feelings of loss around not having a biological child of my own, but I think those feelings would be so much more complicated if I hadn’t had the choice.”
Producer Laura, 31, has stage-four endometriosis, which affects her fertility. Her gynaecologist recommended freezing her eggs before major surgery.

She is in a same-sex relationship, so she knew fertility treatments would probably be part of any parenting plans, even without endometriosis. “Still, it felt quite rushed, because suddenly I was experiencing quite debilitating pain and there was this potential solution of surgery to help minimise that, but in order to have that surgery I needed to freeze my eggs first. It all came at once and felt overwhelming.”

Although Laura had always assumed she would want children, she was anxious. Between the potential for pain and the prospect that the procedure might not work, “I just felt like, oh my God, what am I about to put my body through?”

She went ahead with the freezing, despite her concerns that the process would result in extra pain and potential health complications. As she feared, there were additional issues and she “experienced really awful side-effects during the process. My pain increased significantly, my emotions were out of control. I felt really out of sorts with my body.”

The prospect of needing further fertility treatment to have a child in future is making her rethink her original plan. “I remember being very certain about wanting to have children, but now, actually being faced with the reality, I’m leaning quite far in the other direction.” Knowing her eggs are waiting for her feels more like a burden than a relief. “For me, it’s opened up a can of worms that I just don’t feel prepared to face right now.”

Arts worker Maddison froze her eggs at 37. She was very focused on her career, but worried her ambitions might come at the expense of having children in the future. “I basically thought if I threw money at the problem, I would buy myself some time. I thought I could outsmart biology and hit the stopwatch on it all.”

Looking back, she feels differently: “Now, I feel very critical about how the options were presented to me. Like I said, I threw money at the problem and a lot of people were happy to take it. I didn’t really think about it, but it was painful and the emotional journey was a lot.” The procedure was more gruelling and “isolating” than she had expected, “really hard and uncomfortable. I was single at the time, and it’s a wild ride injecting yourself with those hormones and going through such an invasive process on your own.”

A few years later, in her early 40s, Maddison began experiencing perimenopause symptoms. She decided to stop storing her eggs, because perimenopause “pretty much took having a child off the table”. The ongoing cost of storage – which can be as low as £125 annually in the UK, but in the US and Australia is more like $500-$1,000 a year or more – was also weighing on her. “That kind of made the decision for me.”

Eventually, she met her partner, and became close to his child from a previous relationship. “It’s funny to look back on it all now. I’m in such a different phase of my life, and I have a stepdaughter. You can’t tell someone not to do it, but I would think really hard about it, mainly because of the cost.”
While egg freezing has never been more visible or more popular, research suggests only a small minority of people return to use their eggs. Reports vary, but one
found only “5.7% of women who froze their eggs between 2014 and 2016 returned to use them within the study’s follow-up period of five to seven years”. In Australia,
found that between 2012 and 2021, fewer than 13% of patients with eggs stored returned to use them each year.

Kroener led the research highlighting the low rate of return. She says it is “good biologically” that women are freezing eggs at younger ages, but “younger patients are also the least likely to need their eggs” because they may conceive without help, or with other fertility treatments. “Not coming back isn’t necessarily a bad outcome,” she says.

Jessica Long eventually thawed half her eggs and, after a successful IVF round with them, gave birth to her first child, a daughter, this year. “The process was both surprisingly costly and complicated, and it also delivered exactly what I was hoping for when I signed up for it,” she says. She will continue to pay about US$900 a year for storage, which for her is “a reasonable price to pay” for the potential ability to have another child with her partner.

But what happens if you never use the eggs? For some, this choice can challenge deeply held beliefs. Louise Doherty, 41, is a mental health nurse from Scotland. She froze her eggs at 35 and had a baby through IVF at 41. She is still paying to store her remaining eggs. Although she is pro-choice, she has complicated feelings about her unused eggs. “I want to keep storing them, and hopefully give them all a chance to fertilise and implant, as I don’t like the idea of discarding them or throwing them away,” she says. “This has become even more important to me since having my son. It would feel like I’m throwing away my potential children, as wild as that sounds. I will make sure I always have the money to keep storing them and leave it to my body, to nature, to decide whether they develop and implant in the future,” she adds.

Recalling the disposal of her eggs, Maddison says, “From one perspective, it was a simple admin task, filling in a couple of forms. From the other, it was a fairly devastating moment, finally confronting the idea that I would not be a mother, and at the same time confronting middle-age head on.”

Harraher says that even a clear decision didn’t ease all the heartache. “Once I knew in my heart that I wasn’t going to use my eggs, it took me a long time to actually let them go, and that was very stressful. I was paying the storage fees, which are not insignificant, for many years, knowing I wasn’t going to use these eggs.”

Eventually, she chose to donate them to science. “Having had this kind of health crisis, I felt very comfortable with them going towards medical research and potentially being able to help other people.” The paperwork was still emotional for Harraher, though. “When you release your eggs, you have to do these notarised forms, and I did shed a few tears. But I knew I had made the right decision.”
